Douglas Robinson, ML474658841 Swamp Sparrow audio contributed by Wil Hershberger, ML94352
episodes.transcript: In this episode Why more than a million sandhill cranes, about a third of all the cranes on Earth, stop on one stretch of Nebraska's Platte River every spring Why there are only 15 crane species in the world, and why 11 of them are in trouble How the whooping crane came back from about 21 birds, and why poaching and lost genetic diversity keep that recovery fragile How a fight over the Grayrocks Dam and protections for the whooping crane helped create the Crane Trust and safeguard the Platte What a wet meadow is, why it is so hard to restore, and how cost-share programs with ranchers create crane habitat How a crane's coiled windpipe carries its calls for kilometers, and why cranes cannot live on waste corn alone Scott Taylor: I was working my first spring as a naturalist at Rondeau Provincial Park on the north shore of Lake Erie, one of the largest protected coastal wetlands on the whole side of the lake. It was early, fog still sitting on the marsh, and before I saw anything, I heard them. Sandhill cranes make some of my favorite bird sounds. I don't remember the first time I heard one, but I remember that morning really clearly, and honestly, every time I hear them, it still feels special. Standing near a big flock of them is overwhelming in the best way. Cranes are almost everywhere. Grasslands and wetlands on every continent except South America and Antarctica. Big, loud, impossible to miss. So, you'd be forgiven for assuming there are hundreds of species of them. Can you name every crane on Earth? Don't worry, I got you. Sandhill, Sarus, Grey-crowned, Plus, the whooping crane, demoiselle, brolga, white-naped, Siberian, wattled, blue, black-crowned, hooded, black-necked, red-crowned, and common, sometimes called the Eurasian. Not hundreds, just 15 species, 11 of which are in trouble. Drained wetlands, power lines, turbines, illegal shooting, drought, rising seas, melting permafrost. Cranes are one of the most endangered bird families on Earth. They're also one of the most beloved. Longevity and fidelity in Japan, though if you heard episode one you know where I land on bird fidelity. Immortality in China. Bravery and leadership in South Africa. Divine messengers and omens of spring in Greece. Vigilance across much of Europe. The Celts went the other way entirely. Death, war, betrayal. A king of the underworld who occasionally took crane form. Seeing one was bad news. So, even if you don't know anything about birds, if I asked you to draw a crane, you could probably do a pretty good job. Which brings us to the topic of today's episode, Okay, But... Cranes. To help us unpack that, I'm joined by Dr. Andy Caven, Director of Central Flyway Programs for the International Crane Foundation. After the break, Andy takes us to a river in Nebraska and gives us a number I made him say twice. We get into what a wet meadow actually is and why soggy grassland is worth fighting over. And we talk about what it takes to bring a bird back from almost nothing and how fragile that comeback still is. Stay tuned. Scott Taylor: Welcome back to the podcast, everyone. I'm really excited to have Andy here today to talk all about cranes. Andy, thanks so much for joining us. Andy Caven: Thanks for having me, Scott. Scott Taylor: Yeah, this topic is an exciting one to me. Well, they all are. But I mean, cranes are these amazing, big, recognizable birds that make some of my favorite bird sounds. And I'm wondering if we could start just with what made you fall in love with cranes, especially out of all the birds you could have studied. Andy Caven: Yeah, I feel like sometimes they welcome you in, right? Their charisma, their communication, right? I mean, the 20 plus vocalizations that are distinct, you know, all the different social behaviors, but also their... Everybody talks about umbrella species in ecology, and they're really the real deal. They need so much space, and they're so picky sometimes about what habitats they use that really when you find them, you know you're in a pretty interesting and important space. I think that's what made me first fall in love with them, and then learning more about their natural history and behavior, I was hooked, and all of a sudden I was a crane person. Scott Taylor: Yeah. So I guess, yeah, you've spent years studying the Platte River as this crane stopover site. And I'm wondering, you know, here in Colorado, when we want to see cranes, we either go there or down into Alamosa during the migration period. What's so great about the Platte River in this part of the world that hundreds of thousands or, I guess, is it hundreds of thousands or tens of thousands of these birds stop over? Andy Caven: Oh, it's millions. It's actually I'm working on a new paper that's forthcoming where we use thermal imagery, a big partnership to count them at night before they move. And we had over a million. And I'd previously written a metadata analysis with all the different survey sources and estimated based on math that I thought there was about one point two million at the peak or one point one million. And the thermal survey actually proved that out. One point one to one point three. Scott Taylor: That's like very satisfying as a scientist to be like, I think it's this and I'm going to use math. And then you could just use a camera and be like, yeah, I was right. That's amazing. Million. Wow. Yeah. Andy Caven: Yeah, it was pretty neat. I'm excited for that paper to come out. Bradley Pickens with the US Fish and Wildlife Service was the lead. I think I might be second or third author. It was a big collaborative. But it's not just the biggest gathering of cranes in North America. It's the biggest gathering of cranes in the world. And yeah, it is absolutely the biggest gathering in the world. And what's interesting is there's only 3 million cranes total in the world across all 15 species. Three million. Scott Taylor: Really? I didn't know that. Wow, that's amazing. Scott Taylor: And then there's a million of them all together. Andy Caven: Right in one place right there so three half the cranes in the world of the 15 species there's three million about half the cranes in the world are represented by sandhill cranes and people say oh they're so abundant as not really you know by contrast you know there's you know several six million mallards you know alone right so there's more there's twice as many mallards in north america as there are cranes in the world of all species right so they're rare taxa but the sandhills are the most abundant and even they are such an ecological indicator right although leopold's marshland elegy right like that call means something the interesting thing about flyways most of them follow a river or something right like the mississippi flyway right but the great plains the central flyway is like a stepladder And each one of these east-west rivers that run from, you know, high elevations where you live in Colorado and trickle down into the Missouri Basin, you know, they create a spot to stop. And so you can have big gaps, you know. And I think that kind of promotes congregation. And also the Platte historically, you know, even though it's highly modified and impacted, it's still a reliable place for whooping cranes it's incredibly important too and it was really interesting because a lot it's the only critical habitat for the whooping crane that is privately owned all the rest are state or federal refuges it is privately owned which is why there's ngos up and down that river doing the private lands work, building the preserves. And the Crane Trust, which I used to work for, now I work for the International Crane Foundation. There's only two crane organizations in North America, and I've worked for both. But, you know. Scott Taylor: Nowhere to go next. Just pounce. Hmm. Andy Caven: Where to go next? But the Crane Trust actually was... form based on a lawsuit for the whooping crane in fact in the early endangered species litigations there was a Grayrocks Dam proposed to create energy it was actually building the dam to cool a coal-fired power plant and it was going to pull a significant more water from the headwaters that run into the Platte and to mitigate that they all came to an agreement that they were like okay pay seven million dollars to protect habitat on the Platte we'll call it even And that's what's happened, and that's what created the crane trust. So it's this long history. The conservation history of the Platte is a fascinating thing, too. So I'm waxing away, but I had a big question I used to ask people. I was like, well, did the Platte save the whooping crane, or did the whooping crane save the Platte? Scott Taylor: Yeah. That's interesting to think about.
